newsitem.title: PERU: Peruvian rebels see no end to siege soon.
newsitem.headline: Peruvian rebels see no end to siege soon.

text.p: The leader of Peruvian guerrillas holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence denied on Saturday that a solution to Latin America's longest hostage siege was imminent.
"Unfortunately, that is not the case," Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) leader Nestor Cerpa said in a walkie-talkie conversation from within the residence.
"We still don't foresee a peaceful solution soon ... The positions are still not really drawing close," he added in the conversation that was broadcast on local radio.

Cerpa's comments poured further cold water on speculation in diplomatic and media circles that his 20-strong group of rebels were set to take asylum in Cuba as part of a negotiated agreement to end the 102-day crisis.
"I repeat that we have not come here to look for asylum or a trip abroad," Cerpa insisted, adding the rebels stood firm in their central demand for the freedom of jailed comrades.
"While you hear statements that totally deny the possibility of that (releases), the peaceful solution is very far away," he said.
President Alberto Fujimori has frequently ruled out releasing any MRTA prisoners, and vehmently underlined in a speech on Thursday that no "terrorists" should be allowed to walk free.

But despite the two sides' tough public stances, diplomats, media and officials have been saying all week the government and the MRTA were drawing closer to an accord involving asylum in Cuba and possibly the release of some lower-level prisoners.
"The only thing I can tell you is that the conversations continue," Cerpa said.
The two sides last met face-to-face on March 12, and since then a three-member commission of guarantors has been shuttling between them trying to negotiate a bloodless solution.

Two of the guarantors -- the Vatican's representative Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani and Red Cross representative Michel Minnig -- entered the residence on Saturday for further talks with the MRTA. They left without comment to reporters.
Cerpa's comments followed a similary hard-talking statement on the MRTA's Internet web site managed by its international arm based in Germany.
The statement denounced reports of likely political asylum in Cuba as "government lies that only seek to add to the confusion and hamper a political solution."

Reinforcing the point, rebels inside the mansion scampered across the roof of the building before dawn on Saturday to drape a banner saying, "We shall defend with our lives the freedom of our jailed (comrades)."

In a reminder of the lives at stake, hostage and Peruvian Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela made his first appearance in weeks at the residence on Saturday morning. He was glimpsed looking out of a window which had been blocked by a branch cut down early in the morning by rebels.
Later, Japanese ambassador Morihisa Aoki and another unidentified hostage also appeared at the window.

It was Aoki's cocktail party that the MRTA stormed on Dec. 17, initially taking more than 500 hostages. Most were released in the first weeks of the crisis. The MRTA still holds its most prized bargaining chips, including two cabinet ministers, generals, businessmen, Fujimori's brother Pedro, the ambassadors of Bolivia and Japan, and two dozen Japanese citizens.
The hostages, who have already spent Christmas and New Year's under the rebels' guns, were set to receive a special Mass and traditional gifts of chocolate eggs on Easter Sunday.
Cerpa said the situation was "under control" thanks to regular visits by doctors. He said no hostage would be freed for health or other reasons until "a global solution" was reached.
The captives' only source of news is from local radio stations, where families and supporters have been broadcasting messages and songs all weekend to cheer them up.
